network.tdh.impl.metadataDescription: The Rust core, the Rust and Python references, program B, the Lean model and 6529.io’s backend: how each was written, which conformance vectors it passes, and how they are checked against each other.
network.tdh.impl.title: Implementations
network.tdh.impl.lede: TDH-v1 is one written rule and several programs, written separately from the same text. They run the same test cases and are compared with each other, so a mistake in one shows up as a difference in another.
network.tdh.impl.programs.title: The programs
network.tdh.impl.rust.language: Rust, standard library only, integers only
network.tdh.impl.rust.writtenFrom: Copied from the Rust reference and made into a library, with no rule, arithmetic or decoding code changed. Every copied file is pinned by its hash, and a change to a rule must first be made in P26 and the references.
network.tdh.impl.rust.runsIn: 6529’s daily comparison, since October 15, 2026; 6529.io, from the cutover; every validator, once validators run; proof program A, being built
network.tdh.impl.rust.conformance: The 75 vectors of P26 a4db4ae (1,207 checks) in the validator’s current code, merged October 15, 2026; not yet the 14 of P26’s fifth round. The version the daily job runs follows P26 0621ed4 and passes its 51 vectors (976 checks)
network.tdh.impl.programB.language: Rust, standard library plus a pinned Keccak crate, integers only
network.tdh.impl.programB.writtenFrom: The specifications and the vector files only, in a separate clean room. It never opened the Rust core, the Rust reference or any Python file, and ran the Python reference’s vector runner only as a black box.
network.tdh.impl.programB.runsIn: Proof program B, being built; and, as decided, every validator’s second check before it signs (D125). Not yet inside the validator.
network.tdh.impl.programB.conformance: The 75 vectors of P26 a4db4ae, in the validator’s current code (merged October 15, 2026); not yet the 14 of P26’s fifth round
network.tdh.impl.python.language: Python 3.10 or later, standard library only, no floating point
network.tdh.impl.python.writtenFrom: Written alongside P26 as its reference
network.tdh.impl.python.runsIn: 6529’s daily comparison, since October 15, 2026; any validator, as an optional third check (D125)
network.tdh.impl.python.conformance: All 89 vectors (1,257 checks), at P26 f840096. The daily job runs it at 0621ed4, which had 51
network.tdh.impl.backend.conformance: Not a TDH-v1 implementation: the specification lists where it differs and its issues, measured by replay and by the daily comparison
network.tdh.impl.written.title: How each was written
network.tdh.impl.written.body: The Python reference came first, written with the specification. The Rust reference was then written in a clean room from the specification and the documents it cites, without opening the Python, and it listed every place where it had to choose: 23 in all. P26 now states a rule for each; only the state-read adapter for edition floors stays open.
network.tdh.impl.written.body2: The Rust reference became the validators’ Rust core without any change to its rules. Program B was written later, in a separate clean room, from the specifications only. It found that the first version of D131’s netting let steps inside a transaction change the holdings; P26 made netting uniform the same day, and vectors 45 to 47 pin its three cases. The Lean model was written from P26, definition by definition.
network.tdh.impl.lineage.title: Where each implementation came from
network.tdh.impl.lineage.desc: P26 is the root. The Python reference was written with it. The Rust reference was written from P26 and the documents it cites, without reading the Python, and was copied into the Rust core with no rule changed. Program B was written from the specifications and the vectors only, without opening any other implementation. The Lean model was written from P26. The old backend is replaced by the Rust core at the cutover.

network.tdh.impl.where.caption: Where each implementation runs
network.tdh.impl.checked.title: How they are checked
network.tdh.impl.checked.vectors.title: Conformance vectors.
network.tdh.impl.checked.vectors.body: 89 small cases, each with the exact values the rule must produce: zero holdings, editions, transfers inside one block, transaction netting, consolidation carry, burns, FirstGM, floors, boost tiers, rounding ties, malformed events, the input rules made explicit on October 15 and 16, and inputs that must produce no result. Vectors 1 to 18 were derived by hand (18 updated for D131); 19 to 88 were generated with the reference and their derivations checked by hand. A program conforms when it reproduces every one.
network.tdh.impl.checked.replays.title: Differential replays.
network.tdh.impl.checked.replays.body: Whole days run through more than one implementation and compared with 6529.io’s published values. With D131’s netting, the 2026-10-11 replay reproduces all 10,280 identities and 11,130 wallets; before netting it reproduced 10,278, and the two others were explained (DEV-2).
network.tdh.impl.checked.dual.title: The dual run in every validator.
network.tdh.impl.checked.dual.body: Before it signs, a validator is to compute TDH with the Rust core and with program B. If they disagree on any value, it does not sign and raises an alarm. This is decided (D125) but not yet built in: program B does not run inside the validator yet.
network.tdh.impl.checked.daily.title: The daily comparison.
network.tdh.impl.checked.daily.body: 6529 runs the Rust core and the Python reference every day beside 6529.io’s backend and publishes the three results; the first two days, October 14 and 15, 2026, are published. The Python run reads the Rust run’s own input, after checking its hash, so the two compare computation, not reading Ethereum. The comparison is a separate tool, three_way.py, in the validator code.
network.tdh.impl.checked.proofs.title: Proofs.
network.tdh.impl.checked.proofs.body: Programs A and B are being built to prove each day’s result from Ethereum’s own history in two different zero-knowledge virtual machines; a minimal Ethereum contract that records proven results is built and tested on a copy of mainnet and is not deployed.
network.tdh.impl.checked.after: After the cutover, 6529.io runs the Rust core itself, so comparing the two no longer tests the computation, only its publication. The independent checks are then the Python reference and program B.

network.tdh.impl.anatomy.title: Inside one vector
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.intro: Vector 18, observed on the 2026-10-11 cycle: one transaction sends a held NextGen token out and back. Its addresses are synthetic. A program reads the transfers and the cycle, and must produce exactly the expected values.
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.derivationBody: Both movements of the token are in one transaction, so the transaction is netted (P26 §7.1): wallet c2’s and wallet c3’s net movements are both zero, and nothing moves. Wallet c2 keeps the acquisition it made 239 days before the snapshot, as 6529.io’s backend does. Before D131, the replay applied both movements and restarted the age at 194 days (DEV-2).

network.tdh.impl.checked.difftest.title: Differential tests across four programs.
network.tdh.impl.checked.difftest.body: On October 15, four rounds of generated cycles ran through the Lean model, the Python reference, the Rust core and program B. The first, 40,000 cycles, agreed on every value and differed on whether 20 inputs were valid. The second, 35,000 cases after P26’s clarifications, found the programs disagreeing on which inputs are valid, the Rust core unable to read three registry lists, and the Python reference ignoring one of them in 54 cases. The third, 35,000 cases on P26’s third round, found Lean, Python and program B equal on all 30,000 main cases, and two faults the Rust core had copied from the Rust reference: registry numbers of 2^128 or more, and a cutoff search at the last possible block. P26 settled those findings the same day, and vectors 51 to 74 pin them. The fourth, 35,000 cases on P26’s fourth round, found the Lean model and program B equal on all 30,000 main cases. Two programs differed in how they read the vector files: the Rust core refused 199 inputs whose transfer after the snapshot block, which is not an input, moves 2^128 copies or more (F8, copied from the Rust reference), and the Python reference gave 75 inputs a result although a header timestamp was out of range beside an empty list of raw logs (F9). P26’s fifth round settled both, and a question for the vector format (E12), on October 16 (vectors 76 to 79); the references follow it, and the Rust core and program B have yet to. The validator’s automated checks now run the Rust core against program B on every change.
